sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV — high confidence; a real registration regime)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; a real registration regime
sections.markdown:
**Rhode Island is the outlier of northern New England: it actually requires contractors to register with the state, and chimney work is covered.** The **Contractors' Registration and Licensing Board (CRLB)**, in the Dept. of Business Regulation, administers **R.I. Gen. Laws chapter 5-65**, which requires **every contractor, remodeler, and most subcontractors who build or repair residential/commercial structures and their appurtenances to register before working on a structure (§ 5-65-3)** — and the enumerated subcontractors who must register **explicitly include "Masons, including chimney installers, fireplace installers, and general masonry erectors"**, so chimney work is named in the statute itself. "A city, town, or the state shall not issue a building permit to anyone required to be registered under this chapter who does not have a current, valid registration or valid license" (§ 5-65-3). Registrants must carry **public liability and property damage insurance of $500,000 combined single limit** plus workers' comp as required (§ 5-65-7). **Neither § 5-65-3 nor § 5-65-7 imposes a bond** — do not publish a bond amount. The CRLB line: it **registers** general contractors (no competency exam) and **licenses** only commercial roofers, home inspectors, underground utility, water filtration, well drilling and pump installers — **there is no CRLB chimney license**, so chimney contractors register. Public lookup: **crb.ri.gov/consumer/search-registrantlicensee**.
**Coming: a real residential contractor LICENSE (with an exam), from January 1, 2028.** **P.L. 2025, ch. 421** (S 749A, effective July 2, 2025) added **R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 5-65.4**: "No person shall supervise the construction of a new residential structure or structurally remodel an existing residential structure without proper licensure," **beginning January 1, 2028** (§ 5-65.4-3). "Residential structure" = one- to four-family (§ 5-65.4-2). Applicants must pass a CRLB-approved examination, show insurance, and meet CE; the CRLB must promulgate the program's regulations **on or before January 1, 2027**. "Structurally remodeling" is work "identified by the board as impacting components that support a building's safety or integrity, and any other work identified by the board that requires permits and/or inspections under the state building code" (§ 5-65.4-2) — so whether a **chimney rebuild or reline** needs the new license will turn on the CRLB's 2027 rules (not yet issued). Contractors doing only **nonstructural** home-improvement work stay under registration alone (§ 5-65.4-3). (https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE5/5-65.4/5-65.4-2.htm ; https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE5/5-65.4/5-65.4-3.htm)
**A second, chimney-adjacent credential (DLT, not CRLB):** the Dept. of Labor and Training's pipefitter/sheet-metal rules (**260-RICR-30-15-2, § 2.22(I)**, authority R.I. Gen. Laws § 28-27-7) create a **Decorative Heating Appliances Limited II** license covering "gas fired logs; gas, pellet, or wood decorative appliances and their related flue connections and terminations; replacement flue liners for residential installations only." Applicants **"must hold a current certification from the National Chimney Sweep Guild or the National Fireplace Institute"** plus a notarized statement of two years' experience; fuel piping is not allowed under it, and municipal permits are issued to the licensee. That makes RI one of the rare states where a state license **requires a chimney-industry certification** — but only for that limited appliance/liner scope. *(Whether this license is mandatory for every liner or stove install, versus one route among pipefitter/sheet-metal licenses, is not confirmed — say "a state license for this work exists and requires NCSG or NFI certification," not "required for all liner jobs.")* This is the strongest chimney-relevant credential structure in the batch.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Narrower than the no-license states but still real. CRLB **registration** verifies identity, insurance, and a registry entry — **not flue diagnosis or masonry competence** (registration, unlike specialty licensure, requires no exam — the exam-based ch. 5-65.4 license arrives only on January 1, 2028, and only for new construction and "structural" remodeling). A registered contractor may never have inspected a chimney. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) remain the competence signal, but here "check the registration at crb.ri.gov" is a genuinely useful first step — more than it is in NH/VT/ME.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV — high confidence; explicit chimney + fireplace line items)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; explicit chimney + fireplace line items
sections.markdown: Rhode Island has a **genuinely strong, chimney-naming mandatory disclosure.** **R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-20.8-2** requires the seller of a 1–4 unit residence to deliver a written disclosure **"as soon as practicable, but in any event no later than prior to signing any agreement to transfer"** — and the statute's item list **separately itemizes "Fireplaces — (Number, Working and Maintenance, Defects)" (§ 5-20.8-2(b)(3)(vi)), "Chimney — (Maintenance History, Defects)" ((b)(3)(vii)), and "Heating System — (Type, Imp. & Repairs, Underground Tanks, Zones, Supplemental Heating, Defects, Modifications)" ((b)(3)(xiv)).** Actual-knowledge standard; each violation carries a **civil penalty up to $1,000 per occurrence (§ 5-20.8-5)**. That is a real, chimney-specific disclosure. No general inspection is mandated at transfer (a reported pre-sale smoke/CO certificate is NOT confirmed — see §6); NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: The **Deceptive Trade Practices Act (Unfair Trade Practice and Consumer Protection Act), R.I. Gen. Laws chapter 6-13.1**, gives AG enforcement and a private right of action for damages. Door-to-door sales are separately governed by the **Door-to-Door Sales Act, chapter 6-28**, which covers door-to-door sales of **consumer goods or services of $25 or more** (§ 6-28-2) and gives a **3-day right to cancel — written notice, sent by registered or certified mail, posted not later than midnight three days after signing, excluding Sundays and holidays without mail delivery (§ 6-28-3)** — and **failure to return a deposit lets the buyer recover DOUBLE damages (§ 6-28-4(d))**. That is the exact mechanic against chimney scare-sales. Complaints: RI AG Consumer Protection Unit.

sections.rawHeading: 5 · Permits & codes (GOV — high; a new cycle is legislated)
sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.confidenceNote: high; a new cycle is legislated
sections.markdown: Rhode Island has a **statewide State Building Code**; the one- and two-family code **RISBC-2 (510-RICR-00-00-2) adopts the 2021 IRC** with RI amendments (current version effective Dec 1, 2025 on the Secretary of State's rules site). **Chapter 10 (Chimneys and Fireplaces) is adopted with no RI changes; IRC R315 is deleted — "Carbon Monoxide Alarms are governed by the Rhode Island Fire Safety Code" (450-RICR-00-00-1 through -10)** (https://rules.sos.ri.gov/regulations/part/510-00-00-2). **Next cycle is set by statute: P.L. 2026, ch. 377/378 (H 7774A / companion, enacted June 19, 2026) amends R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-27.3-100.1.5 so the 2024 IRC "shall take effect for one- to three-family dwelling units not later than January 1, 2027"** (https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/PublicLaws/law26/law26377.htm) — re-check which edition is in force at publish. Because registration is tied to permits (§ 5-65-3 bars permits to unregistered contractors), chimney relines, rebuilds, crowns, and solid-fuel appliance installs that require a permit also require a registered contractor. Routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not permit work. RI is small and comparatively uniform, so less local patchwork than the other three states.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — framework confirmed; pre-sale certificate NOT FOUND in primary sources — do not publish it)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.confidenceNote: framework confirmed; pre-sale certificate NOT FOUND in primary sources — do not publish it
sections.markdown:
**What the primary sources confirm:**
- Smoke and CO alarms in one-, two- and three-family homes are governed by the **RI Fire Safety Code**, not the building code. RISBC-2 deletes IRC R315 and says "Carbon Monoxide Alarms are governed by the Rhode Island Fire Safety Code" (https://rules.sos.ri.gov/regulations/part/510-00-00-2).
- The Fire Safety Code administrative rule says the Fire Safety Code "sets forth the requirements for smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms in all one (1), two (2) and three (3) family dwellings in the State" (450-RICR-00-00-1 § 1.2(B), eff. March 1, 2026; https://rules.sos.ri.gov/regulations/part/450-00-00-1).
- The RI Fire Code states that its "application to one- and two-family dwellings and three family apartment buildings is strictly limited to the installation of smoke detection and carbon monoxide detection as set forth in RIGL § 23-28.1-2(b)(2)(i)" (450-RICR-00-00-7 § 1.3.1.1, eff. March 1, 2026; https://rules.sos.ri.gov/regulations/part/450-00-00-7).
- **R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-28.1-2(b)(2)** excludes private 1–3 family dwellings from the general fire code except for smoke/CO detection standards. It caps the local fire authority's fee for "smoke alarm and carbon monoxide alarm plan review together with any subsequent detection inspections" at **$75 (one-family) / $125 (two-family) / $175 (three-family)** (https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE23/23-28.1/23-28.1-2.htm; latest amendment P.L. 2016, ch. 472).
- The old standalone chapters **23-28.34 ("Fire and Carbon Monoxide Detection Systems")** and **23-28.35 ("Fire Detectors and Carbon Monoxide Systems in Existing Residential Occupancies")** are **repealed**.

**What is NOT confirmed — do not publish:** an earlier draft said that at transfer of title the seller must give the buyer a local fire-department certificate of smoke/CO compliance, inspected within 60 days, for a ~$30 fee. None of these primary sources mentions any sale or transfer requirement, certificate, 60-day window or $30 fee:
- § 23-28.1-2
- 450-RICR-00-00-1 (administrative), -7 (Fire Code), -8 (Life Safety Code) and -10 (Fire Alarm Code)

The requirement may still exist in a part not reached, such as the NFPA 1 text incorporated by reference or local practice. Until a primary source is found, the page may say only this: "Rhode Island's Fire Safety Code sets smoke and CO alarm standards for 1–3 family homes; ask your local fire department what it requires when a home is sold."

**Unconfirmed as well:** the exact trigger conditions (fuel-burning appliance, fireplace, attached garage) for 1–2 family homes. That text lives in the incorporated code, which was not reached.

A permitted chimney or stove job is still the natural moment to check alarms.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: Rhode Island has meaningful but lower wood-heat share than NH/VT/ME. No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime beyond federal EPA new-stove standards (NATIONAL STANDARD). Not a material statutory section for RI; 1–2 sentences and move on.

sections.rawHeading: 8 · Scam landscape (REF — partial; pull specifics before publish)
sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The RI AG's Consumer Protection Unit pursues home-improvement fraud, and the door-knock "we were in the neighborhood / noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook chapter 6-28 + 6-13.1 violation; here it is **also** an unregistered-contractor problem, since unregistered work is barred under § 5-65-3. Regional New England reporting has tied chimney-sweep scams to weak trade regulation elsewhere — but RI's CRLB is the counterexample. **Specific RI chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT YET CONFIRMED — re-run search before publish.**

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: Rhode Island **BREAKS the master correlation — and breaks it in the "strong-on-both" direction that's rarer than the weak-on-both cases.** The rule predicts a state either licenses hard and discloses little, or licenses nothing and discloses a lot. Rhode Island does **both**: it requires contractors (masons included) to register with the CRLB and bars permits to the unregistered, AND its seller-disclosure form names the chimney and the fireplace as separate line items, AND its fire-safety code (not the building code) owns smoke/CO alarm standards for 1–3 family homes. And it is getting stronger: from **January 1, 2028**, new-home builders and "structural" remodelers need an exam-based CRLB **license** (ch. 5-65.4). For a state this small, that is an unusually complete consumer stack. (Do not claim a pre-sale fire-department CO certificate — see §6.) The catch the page should flag: CRLB **registration** carries no competency exam, so "registered" still is not "qualified" — which is exactly the gap individual certs and an independent audit fill.

h1: Rhode Island chimney & fireplace laws: know your rights
metaDescription: Rhode Island chimney & fireplace laws: licensing, seller disclosure, right to cancel and CO alarm rules, with statutes cited.

season.note: Coastal southern-New-England climate, milder than NH/VT/ME. Burn season ~Nov–Mar. Rush: SEP–NOV. Best booking: APR–JUN.

faq.q: What should I check before hiring a chimney company in Rhode Island?
faq.a: State licensing: YES-ish — CRLB REGISTRATION required (R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-65-3; "masons, including chimney installers, fireplace installers"; no exam; no CRLB chimney license) + DLT Decorative Heating Appliances Limited II license requiring NCSG/NFI cert (260-RICR-30-15-2.22(I)) + NEW residential contractor LICENSE with exam for new 1–4 family construction and "structural" remodeling from 1/1/2028 (ch. 5-65.4, P.L. 2025 ch. 421; scope set by CRLB rules due 1/1/2027). Registration or credential: YES — CRLB registry, permits barred to unregistered contractors. Seller disclosure at sale: YES — § 5-20.8-2, form names Fireplaces + Chimney + Heating separately (penalty $1,000/occurrence). Right to cancel a sale made at your home: YES (Door-to-Door Sales Act § 6-28-3; goods or services ≥ $25; notice by registered/certified mail; double damages for unreturned deposit § 6-28-4(d)). Carbon monoxide alarm law: Fire Safety Code sets smoke/CO alarm standards for 1–3 family homes (RISBC-2 defers R315; § 23-28.1-2(b)(2)); a pre-sale fire-dept certificate was reported but NOT found in primary sources — do not publish it. Where to check a contractor: crb.ri.gov + riag.ri.gov complaints. Then ask the eight questions below, get the inspection findings in writing with photos, and never sign for "emergency" work on the day of a door-knock.

faq.q: Is a chimney inspection required when a home sells in Rhode Island?
faq.a: Rhode Island has a genuinely strong, chimney-naming mandatory disclosure. R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-20.8-2 requires the seller of a 1–4 unit residence to deliver a written disclosure "as soon as practicable, but in any event no later than prior to signing any agreement to transfer" — and the statute's item list separately itemizes "Fireplaces — (Number, Working and Maintenance, Defects)" (§ 5-20.8-2(b)(3)(vi)), "Chimney — (Maintenance History, Defects)" ((b)(3)(vii)), and "Heating System — (Type, Imp. & Repairs, Underground Tanks, Zones, Supplemental Heating, Defects, Modifications)" ((b)(3)(xiv)).

faq.q: Can I cancel a chimney contract I signed at my door in Rhode Island?
faq.a: The Deceptive Trade Practices Act (Unfair Trade Practice and Consumer Protection Act), R.I. Gen. Laws chapter 6-13.1, gives AG enforcement and a private right of action for damages. Door-to-door sales are separately governed by the Door-to-Door Sales Act, chapter 6-28, which covers door-to-door sales of consumer goods or services of $25 or more (§ 6-28-2) and gives a 3-day right to cancel — written notice, sent by registered or certified mail, posted not later than midnight three days after signing, excluding Sundays and holidays without mail delivery (§ 6-28-3) — and failure to return a deposit lets the buyer recover DOUBLE damages (§ 6-28-4(d)).
